trial_name: CRASH-3 — Tranexamic Acid vs Placebo in Adults with Acute TBI within 3 Hours of Injury
citation: The CRASH-3 trial collaborators. Effects of tranexamic acid on death, disability, vascular occlusive events and other morbidities in patients with acute traumatic brain injury (CRASH-3): a randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2019;394:1713–23.
one_liner: Early TXA within 3 hours of TBI modestly reduces head injury-related death, particularly in patients with mild-to-moderate injury and reactive pupils, without clear increase in vascular events.

pico.population: Adults with acute TBI within 3 hours of injury, GCS ≤12 or intracranial bleeding on CT, no major extracranial bleeding, where clinician is substantially uncertain about TXA.
pico.intervention: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV loading dose over 10 minutes followed by 1 g IV infusion over 8 hours.
pico.comparison: Matching placebo (same volume and infusion schedule).
pico.outcome: Primary: head injury-related death in hospital within 28 days among those treated within 3 hours.

background.existing_knowledge: Progressive intracranial haemorrhage after TBI is common and associated with raised ICP, herniation, death, and disability. Haemorrhage expansion occurs mainly in the first hours, providing a time-critical window for haemostatic intervention. TXA is an antifibrinolytic with proven efficacy in surgical bleeding and in reducing bleeding deaths in trauma with major extracranial haemorrhage (CRASH-2). Prior to CRASH-3, two small RCTs in TBI showed a possible mortality reduction (RR 0.63; 95% CI 0.40–0.99).
background.knowledge_gap: Lack of high-quality evidence on efficacy and safety of TXA specifically in isolated TBI, especially regarding disability outcomes and risk of vascular occlusive events.
background.hypothesis: Early TXA reduces head injury-related death and disability in adults with acute TBI, with greatest benefit when given within 3 hours and in patients with less severe injury.

methods.design: Pragmatic, international, multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind superiority trial.
methods.setting: 175 hospitals across 29 countries; enrolment from emergency departments/acute hospital settings.

inclusion: Adults with TBI within 3 hours of injury (amended from 8h)
GCS ≤12 OR any intracranial bleeding on CT
Clinician substantially uncertain about TXA appropriateness
exclusion: Clinician not substantially uncertain (TXA clearly indicated or contraindicated)

methods.intervention: TXA 1 g IV loading dose over 10 min, then 1 g IV infusion over 8 h.
methods.comparison: Matching placebo (same volume and infusion schedule).
methods.blinding: Double-blind; identical treatment packs numbered, allocation by selecting a pack from a box; patients, clinicians, outcome assessors masked.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 10,000 to provide 90% power (two-sided alpha 1%) to detect 15% relative mortality reduction (20% to 17%). After protocol change to treat-within-3h, target increased to 13,000 to ensure ~10,000 treated within 3 h. Final: 12,737 randomised, 9,202 treated within 3 h.
methods.primary_outcome: Head injury-related death in hospital within 28 days among patients treated within 3 hours of injury (amended primary analysis population).
secondary_outcomes: Vascular occlusive events (composite of MI, stroke, PE, DVT)
Disability at discharge/28 days: inability to wash or dress, and Disability Rating Scale (DRS) score among survivors
methods.follow_up: Outcomes assessed in hospital up to 28 days (or earlier discharge); disability recorded at discharge/day 28.

headline_bullets: In the prespecified within-3h population, TXA showed a modest reduction in head injury-related death (RR 0.94; 95% CI 0.86–1.02), with larger effect after excluding moribund patients (RR 0.89; 0.80–1.00).
Benefit signals were concentrated in patients with milder injury severity proxies (GCS 9–15; both pupils reactive), suggesting TXA prevents expansion of salvageable intracranial haemorrhage.
Major safety outcomes showed no clear excess vascular occlusive events; seizure estimates compatible with no effect and modest harm.
The effect on head injury-related death within 24h (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.69–0.95) supports a timely mechanism on early bleeding-related deaths.

outcomes_table.outcome: Primary: head injury-related death within 28 days (treated within 3h, ITT)
Sensitivity: head injury-related death (treated within 3h, excluding GCS 3 and bilateral unreactive pupils)
Disability: unable to wash or dress (within 3h)

outcomes_table.note: Continuous disability measure; no between-group estimate

safety: Vascular occlusive events: 69/4613 (1.5%) TXA vs 60/4514 (1.3%) placebo; RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.80–1.59.
No other major safety signals reported.

domains.notes: Concealed, identical packs, allocation by selection from a box; baseline characteristics well balanced.
Double-blind; only 13 patients unblinded (6 TXA, 7 placebo), unlikely to bias mortality outcomes.
Minimal missing data (0.8% in each group for primary outcome); ITT analysis.
High adherence: loading dose given to 98.6% TXA vs 98.7% placebo; maintenance dose 93.4% vs 92.9%.
Balanced age (mean 41.7 vs 41.9), sex (81.1% male both), and GCS/pupil reactivity categories.
Clinician-assigned cause of death, masked but inherently subjective; non-differential misclassification may attenuate observed effects.
Mid-trial amendment reduced time window from 8h to 3h and focused primary analysis on within-3h population; conducted blind to outcome data but complicates interpretation.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity is moderate-to-strong: randomisation and masking were robust, adherence high, missing data minimal, but confidence is tempered by mid-trial protocol/endpoint modification and reliance on clinician-assigned cause of death.

domains.notes: Broad international adult TBI population (29 countries, mean age ~42, 80% male); includes wide severity range.

Simple IV intervention feasible in ED/prehospital settings; benefit time-dependent (<3h). Excludes major extracranial bleeding, so polytrauma with haemorrhagic shock requires caution (better informed by CRASH-2).
Children, penetrating TBI, delayed presentation >3h, and patients where TXA clearly indicated/contraindicated were excluded.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is good for adult blunt TBI patients who can receive IV TXA rapidly within 3h and without major extracranial bleeding.

strengths: Very large, international, pragmatic randomised trial with double-blind placebo control.
High protocol adherence to TXA dosing regimen, strong separation between study arms.
Low missing data for primary outcome; prespecified sensitivity analysis to mitigate dilution by non-salvageable patients.
Clinically implementable intervention with a clear biologically plausible time-sensitive mechanism.
limitations: Protocol amendment restricted enrolment time window (8h to 3h) and modified primary analysis during the trial, increasing interpretive complexity.
Primary endpoint relied on clinician classification of cause of death; non-differential misclassification could attenuate observed effects.
Disability outcomes assessed at discharge/28 days, potentially too early to capture long-term recovery.
Thromboembolic event capture used high-specificity criteria (imaging/post-mortem), which may underestimate total events but is less likely to bias relative comparisons.

critical_appraisal.summary: CRASH-3 is a large, well-conducted trial suggesting early TXA modestly reduces head injury-related death, especially in milder TBI, with acceptable safety. Confidence is somewhat limited by mid-trial amendments and outcome ascertainment, but overall moderate-to-strong internal validity and good generalisability.
strengths: Prespecified sensitivity analysis mitigating dilution by non-salvageable cases
weaknesses: Protocol amendment during trial complicates interpretation
Early disability assessment may not reflect long-term outcomes
Vascular event ascertainment may underestimate true incidence

sections.authors_conclusion: Early TXA should be considered for eligible adult TBI patients, especially those with mild-to-moderate injury and reactive pupils, to reduce head injury-related death; no clear excess vascular occlusive events, but seizure risk remains uncertain.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: CRASH-3 supports early TXA (within 3h) in adult TBI, particularly in patients with mild-to-moderate injury and reactive pupils, to reduce head injury-related death without major safety concerns.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult blunt TBI patients with GCS ≤12 or intracranial bleeding on CT, who can receive IV TXA within 3h of injury, without significant extracranial bleeding.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: TXA is not proven to improve functional disability; should not replace standard neurocritical care or be used in severe moribund TBI.
implementation_caveats: Time-critical: benefit plausibly within 3h; systems must minimise delay.
Dose: 1g bolus over 10min, then 1g infusion over 8h.
Seizure risk may be slightly increased; monitor.
Exclude patients with known contraindications or where TXA clearly indicated/contraindicated per clinician judgement.

controversies.notes: Lancet Comment: 28-day head injury-related mortality biases toward null; early bleeding-related endpoints and optimal dosing remain uncertain. VTE under-ascertainment possible.
Correspondence cautioned against over-interpreting mild-to-moderate subgroup, citing heterogeneity in severe TBI, instability of early GCS/pupils, and need for stringent interaction thresholds.
Earlier-treated patients may be more severely injured, confounding 'earlier is better' analyses; supports need for adjusted models.
Concerns about misclassification with cause-specific outcome; investigators argued blind allocation biases misclassification toward null, not creating spurious benefit.
Investigators explained that misclassification would bias towards null, defended interaction testing, and addressed time-to-treatment confounding.

Post-CRASH-3 evidence generally supportive of early TXA for selected TBI; greatest plausibility in mild-to-moderate injury; uncertainty persists in severe injury, delayed treatment, and prehospital delivery.

context_related_trials.relation: Demonstrated TXA reduces bleeding deaths in trauma with major extracranial haemorrhage, establishing safety and efficacy in polytrauma; CRASH-3 extends evidence to isolated TBI.

unresolved_questions: Optimal TXA dosing regimen (single bolus vs continued infusion, higher doses)?
Efficacy and safety in severe TBI with fixed pupils?
Long-term functional and cognitive outcomes beyond 28 days?
Effect in pediatric and penetrating TBI?

numbers_to_remember: Mild-to-moderate GCS: RR 0.78 (0.64–0.95); reactive pupils: RR 0.87 (0.77–0.98)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: For adults with TBI within 3h, give TXA 1g IV bolus + 1g infusion; it modestly reduces head injury-related death, especially if GCS 9-15 and pupils reactive, without clear excess vascular events.
